method: Read and solve only the allowed seed prose and selected definitions, after the required skill, review-order, and contract instructions. No author solution, key, question view, draft, prior review, binding packet, product lesson, or referenced earlier exercise was opened. Establish the elementary derivatives directly from difference quotients and apply the selected sum theorem, repeatedly for three terms.
elementary_derivations: For a real constant c, ((x+t)+c-(x+c))/t=1 for t!=0, so (x+c)'=1. A constant alone has difference quotient (c-c)/t=0 and derivative 0.
For x^2, ((x+t)^2-x^2)/t=2x+t for t!=0, so (x^2)'=2x at every real x.
For 1/x, x must be nonzero. For sufficiently small nonzero t with x+t!=0, (1/(x+t)-1/x)/t=-1/(x(x+t)). Its limit is -1/x^2.

For sqrt(x) at x>0, choose sufficiently small nonzero t with x+t>0. Rationalization gives (sqrt(x+t)-sqrt(x))/t=1/(sqrt(x+t)+sqrt(x)). Its limit is 1/(2sqrt(x)). No derivative of sqrt(x) at x=0 is needed for this seed, because the accompanying 1/x already excludes zero.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Part a: f(x)=x+5 has derivative f'(x)=1 for all real x. Its difference quotient is ((x+t)+5-(x+5))/t=t/t=1. Part b: g(x)=x^2+3 has derivative g'(x)=2x for all real x. The quadratic difference quotient is 2x+t and the constant contributes 0, so the selected sum theorem gives 2x+0=2x. Thus neither added constant contributes to either derivative.

Part a: h(x)=x^2+x has derivative h'(x)=2x+1 for all real x. The two summands have derivatives 2x and 1, and the selected sum theorem adds them. Independently its full difference quotient is 2x+t+1, tending to 2x+1. Part b: u(x)=x^2+x+7 has derivative u'(x)=2x+1 for all real x. The added constant has derivative 0; the full difference quotient is again 2x+t+1. Both functions therefore have the same derivative despite different values.

Part a: v(x)=x^2+1/x+5 has real domain x!=0. At every such x the derivative is v'(x)=2x-1/x^2. The reciprocal difference quotient is -1/(x(x+t)), so the full quotient is 2x+t-1/(x(x+t)); its limit is 2x-1/x^2. The constant 5 contributes zero. Part b: y(x)=x^2+1/x+sqrt(x) has real domain x>0, since the square root requires x>=0 and the reciprocal excludes zero. At every x>0, y'(x)=2x-1/x^2+1/(2sqrt(x)). The full difference quotient, after rationalizing the root term, is 2x+t-1/(x(x+t))+1/(sqrt(x+t)+sqrt(x)), whose limit is the stated derivative. There is no domain point at x=0 and no real domain point at negative x for part b.

Let u and v be functions on the same interval, differentiable at a common point x, and let w=u-v. For every sufficiently small nonzero increment t allowed by that interval, (w(x+t)-w(x))/t=(u(x+t)-u(x))/t-(v(x+t)-v(x))/t. The first quotient tends to u'(x) and the second to v'(x), both finite by the differentiability assumption. The difference of these limits therefore exists and equals u'(x)-v'(x). By the definition of derivative, w'(x)=u'(x)-v'(x). Since x was arbitrary among common differentiability points, (u-v)'=u'-v' throughout that set. This proves the source assertion directly without assuming the subtraction rule being proved. Consistently with the selected sum theorem, the quotient for -v is the negative of v's quotient, so (-v)'=-v' and u-v=u+(-v) yields the same result.

The separate proof task establishes differentiability of the difference using the two existing finite derivative limits.
